claims.text: Cryogenic rolling followed by controlled low-temperature annealing can produce a hierarchical microstructure in a eutectic high-entropy alloy.
The treatment will refine initially coarse lamellar colonies while preserving their dual-phase lamellar architecture.
The hierarchical microstructure will contain ultrafine grains within the lamellae.
The hierarchical microstructure will have a higher density of grain and phase boundaries than the baseline.
A conventionally processed EHEA has coarse dual-phase lamellar colonies with continuous internal boundaries prone to microcrack initiation at room temperature.
Cryogenic rolling increases stored strain energy and introduces deformation-induced defects.
Controlled annealing after cryogenic rolling can produce partial recrystallization and refinement without complete grain growth.
The processing requires a cryogenic-rolling thickness reduction greater than approximately 80–90%.
The annealing temperature should be low enough to avoid complete recrystallization.
The refined hierarchy and increased interface population arrest or retard microcrack propagation.
Refined grain size enhances work hardening.
Crack arrest and grain-refinement strengthening act synergistically to improve both strength and ductility.
Cryogenic rolling and annealing can simultaneously enhance yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and room-temperature tensile elongation.
The increases in strength and ductility will be statistically significant relative to a warm-rolled and annealed baseline.
Warm-rolled and annealed baseline samples have high strength but limited ductility because microcracks initiate at coarse, continuous lamellar boundaries.
Preservation or inheritance of the duplex lamellar structure is important to the beneficial strength–ductility response.
Excessively high annealing temperatures that cause complete recrystallization or lamellar coarsening may abolish the benefit.
The intervention is applicable only to alloy chemistries capable of forming a duplex lamellar structure.
The hypothesis can be tested by comparing cryo-rolled and annealed specimens with warm-rolled and annealed specimens from the same alloy using tensile tests and SEM/TEM characterization.

Failure to obtain both a statistically significant strength increase and a statistically significant ductility increase, or failure to produce the proposed refined hierarchy, falsifies the hypothesis.
